# Raised Beds

## Overview

Three beds along the south wall of the vegetable patch, built one autumn and filled over a fortnight. They replaced a strip of tired lawn that never drained well and always flooded at the low corner. The whole job cost less than a shed and has outlasted two of my wheelbarrows. The beds sit on a gentle slope, so each one is levelled with a small retaining lip on the downhill side to stop the soil washing out.

## Building the Beds

I started by pegging out the layout with string lines, running two long beds parallel to the wall and a third crossways at the end to close the square. Everything is set on a 60 cm path so I can push a barrow between rows without treading on the soil and compacting it. The frames are built from untreated cedar boards, which weather grey but do not rot for years and never need stain or oil to survive our wet winters. Each bed measures 2.4 m by 1.2 m by 30 cm, a size I chose because it lets me reach the middle from either side without climbing in. I cut the boards square, drilled pilot holes to stop the cedar splitting, and screwed the corners into 75 mm posts driven 40 cm into the ground so the panels stay straight when the soil presses outward. The frames went down level, checked with a long spirit level across the diagonal, and the corners came out square within a few millimetres. I set the long sides first and measured both diagonals before I drove the posts, since a twisted frame is almost impossible to pull straight once the fill is pressing on it. A brush of linseed oil on the sawn ends was the only finish I bothered with, and only on the two frames facing the weather.

Once the frames were standing I knocked the turf off the base and laid cardboard sheet mulch straight onto the ground, overlapping the seams by 20 cm so nothing pushes up through the joins. Over the cardboard I buried split logs at the base, laying them loosely across the width, and topped that with the sods I had lifted, turned upside down so the roots die off. The logs soak up winter rain and rot slowly, feeding the bed from underneath and holding moisture through dry spells. This layer also means I need far less fill than if I had simply filled the whole box with bought soil, and it saved me three trips to the yard with the trailer.

The growing layer is a mix of topsoil and compost at roughly 60:40, wheeled in barrow by barrow and trodden lightly as it went in so it settles without compacting hard. I raked the surface flat and left it to sit for two weeks before planting anything, which let the level drop by a few centimetres as the fill knitted together. That first winter the beds froze solid for a week and the cardboard underneath softened, so the worms moved in quickly and by spring the fill had turned into a decent dark loam full of life. On the heavy bed at the shaded end I stirred a bag of grit through the top layer, because that corner holds water long after the rest has drained and I wanted the roots to breathe.

Before I filled the last bed I dug a shallow trench around the inside of the frame and lined it with 6 mm galvanised hardware cloth, folded up the sides, so voles cannot tunnel in from the hedge along the wall. It sits below the surface where it will not catch a fork, and the edges tuck under the frame so there is no gap left open. Then I finished with a straw mulch about five centimetres deep across the whole surface, which keeps weeds down and stops the rain capping the soil into a crust. I left a small gap at the frame edge so slugs have fewer damp corners to hide in through the summer. The mulch gets topped up each autumn from the straw bales I keep behind the shed, and the old layer is forked in when it has rotted down.

## Planting

Garlic goes in the front bed in October, cloves pushed in point up, ten centimetres apart and two deep. Kale fills the middle bed over winter and crops until spring. Beans go in the back bed once the soil warms, climbing a frame of canes, with the lower leaves stripped so air moves through.
